task: This is a synthetic exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes as the fixed record: select, organize and phrase the story without inventing additional reported events, scenes, quotations or reporting activity. Write a headline and an explainer of roughly 450–650 words in AP style for general newspaper readers answering how Fenwick Reach chooses which curb ramps to rebuild first. Write from this reporting snapshot as of September 18, 2026.

facts.text: The fictional Fenwick Reach access office received 48 reports concerning 28 distinct curb-ramp locations during its latest review period.
Several reports concerned the same location, so the number of reports is not the number of separate ramps needing work.
The current capital program funds work at 16 locations drawn from resident reports and city inspections; other identified needs await assessment or later budgets.
The city prioritizes connected routes to public buildings, transport stops and frequently used services rather than simply ranking complaint totals.
Inspectors record slope, available turning space, drainage and obstructions such as utility covers at each location.
A ramp can appear on the list because of a problem with its approach or landing, even when its sloping surface looks intact.
Access engineer Rina Voss said, "A usable ramp on one corner does not complete a journey if the next corner still stops you."
The city's current design guide supplies the criteria for these projects; the packet does not offer a legal compliance determination for every existing ramp.
Locations requiring drainage changes or utility relocation need coordinated work rather than a simple surface replacement.
The $365,000 program budget includes design and associated street work, not an equal cash allowance assigned to each ramp.
The city has not published a final construction cost for every individual location.
A mobility advisory group asked the city to show the route connections that explain its choices, not only a list of selected corners.
Group member Pera Linn said, "We want to see the path that becomes possible, not just sixteen completed entries on a spreadsheet."
Residents can provide information about destinations and recurring access barriers during the review, without disclosing a medical diagnosis.
The office does not treat the absence of a complaint as evidence that a ramp is usable.
The office has not supplied the overlap between the 28 reported locations and the 16 funded locations, which also draw on city inspections.
Temporary arrangements during construction will be announced separately for each site.
Completion of the 16 projects will not establish that the entire street network is accessible.
The city will publish a map linking selected locations to the intended routes before work begins.
Some older ramp entries use intersection names that changed after two streets were combined, requiring staff to reconcile duplicate records.
The advisory group will review completed routes with staff after construction, rather than certify them in advance from drawings alone.
The packet contains no prediction of increased pedestrian counts or a quantified benefit for all users.

forbidden_additions: Forty-eight distinct ramps or work at every reported site.
An equal per-ramp cost, advance legal certification or a fully accessible network.
A medical-disclosure requirement or quantified usage benefit.
Exactly 12 reported locations said to remain unfunded without knowing the overlap with the funded list.
preserve: Connected routes and physical constraints as reasons for prioritization.
Reports, locations and funded projects as different counts.
Exact quotation wording and attribution when quotations are used.
